newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AWF third 1997/98 Australia wheat f'cast 17.85 MT.
newsitem.headline: AWF third 1997/98 Australia wheat f'cast 17.85 MT.

text.p: Private forecaster Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd (AWF) has held its forecast for Australia's 1997/98 wheat crop virtually steady with its forecast of a month ago, at 17.85 million tonnes.
AWF's previous crop forecast was 17.89 million tonnes.

The AWF forecast is now on the low end of official and unofficial forecasts, with the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) earlier this week raising its forecast to 19.2 million tonnes from 17.8 million and the trade widely expecting a crop of about 19 million tonnes.

Sowing operations are in progress in all states. Subsoil moisture was favourable for most of Queensland but in many areas more soil moisture was required for seed to have a good chance of germinating, AWF managing director Brian Bailey said.
Sowings were continuing but would probably have to pause soon if there were no follow-up rain, he said. About 30mm was all that was required in most areas of Queensland.
New South Wales (NSW) now had enough rain for sowing to proceed to completion, Bailey said.
In the north of the state there was already good subsoil moisture and enough rain in the third week of May for sowings to start. They are continuing now, Bailey said.
The southwest of NSW was one area with poor subsoil moisture and had not yet had enough rain to sow wheat on, he said.
Growers were sowing other early crops such as canola, triticale and lupins, in the hope of further rains before mid-June.
The NSW wheat crop was being seeded close to optimum dates, he said.

Victoria had had enough rain for widespread sowings in both the Wimmera and Mallee districts, while growers in the western Mallee were choosing to wait before seeding wheat, AWF said. The growers want more rain and to postpone flowering later to reduce the risk of frost damage in spring, the forecaster said.

South Australia has not yet been able to do much seeding of wheat except in the southeast, a minor grain producing area, Bailey said. Growers have seeded oats and lupins into dry soil and are currently drilling fertiliser before sowing wheat on the next rain, he said.
Western Australia has had excellent opening rains, which have favoured the northern agricultural areas where sowing is nearly complete, AWF said.
The southern areas are also being sown into good soil moisture, about five weeks ahead of sowings in southern grain areas last year.
